newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria c.bank mulls bank closures by end-Oct.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria c.bank mulls bank closures by end-Oct.

text.p: Bulgaria's central bank is expected to decide this month which of the nine local commercial banks placed under special supervision last month to allow to seek insolvency through the courts, a banker said on Monday.

"The Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) will review sequestrators' reports on the nine banks' financial state and decide for which of them to seek bankruptcy procedures through the courts," a BNB senior official, who declined to be named, told Reuters.

On September 23 the BNB placed under special supervision nine banks with negative capital to risk assets ratios ranging from minus two percent for Elitbank to minus 56.6 percent for Economic Bank, way down on Basel banking standards of eight percent.
Delayed settlement payments of the nine banks totaled 11.4 billion levs.
The sequestrators' reports are due be presented at the central bank by October 16.
"The central bank so far did not see any serious reasons to ease its restrictive measures over banks," said the official.
"Only the Economic bank and the Balkanbank might avoid a bankruptcy procedure due to investors' interest in them," the official added.
The biggest and most stable of Bulgaria's banks, state-owned Bulbank, is expected to submit this week its offer for buying 66.7 percent in the Economic Bank.

The South Korean concern Daewoo Corp has shown interest in buying ailing Balkanbank once Daewoo experts have evaluated its condition. Both Economic Bank and Balkanbank are included the list of nine banks.
Last week four of the nine banks under special supervision -- the Trade & Savings Bank (TSBank), Mollov, Businessbank, and Dobrudzha Bank, appealed to the Supreme Court against the BNB decision.

Their appeals are based on memorandums signed between 19 banks and the BNB in June, under which the BNB received detailed information of their state and the banks pledged to improve collection of non-performing loans. The memorandums did not include any special supervision options.

Businessbank's negative capital to risk assets ratio stood at minus 9.95 percent, Mollov bank's ratio was minus 19 percent. Dobrudzha bank's negative capital adequacy was estimated at minus 54.06 percent.

The private Trade & Savings Bank has no negative capital to assets ratio, but heavily depended on refinancing from the BNB and the State Savings Bank due to delayed settlement payments of 4.8 billion levs by September 23.
Under Bulgarian banking laws the central bank can hold a bank under special supervision for no longer than one year. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
